paragraphs: §1 — The frame of the polemic

The matters in which they disagree would be some fifty, and we have no need to mention them all. We wish to mention of them the grave ones — those which oblige each group of them to ascribe to the other group, in the matter in which it dissented, the abandonment of the religion. For the dissension between the two groups in this matter is not less than what lies between the two groups together and the rest of the Karaites and the ʿAnanites. In this is the annulment of the "tradition" (qabbalah) they claim, and [of the claim] that their doctrines are taken from prophecy.

Before we recount what they dispute among themselves, let us recount their statement on this matter. [They said:] that "Bayt Hillel" and "Bayt Shammai" dissented in [various] matters — some in which "Bayt Shammai" were lenient and "Bayt Hillel" stringent, and some in which "Bayt Hillel" were lenient and "Bayt Shammai" stringent. And the Rabbanites said: one who acted by what "Bayt Shammai" made stringent and by what "Bayt Hillel" made lenient would be a sinner; and likewise if he acted by what "Bayt Shammai" made lenient and "Bayt Hillel" stringent. The obligation [they held]: to act by one of the two statements, in its stringency and its leniency together. And one who inclined to one of the two parties altogether was approved. Had their scandal appeared in no [other] point than this, it would suffice to leap [at it]; for they made two contradictory statements both true, and held that whoever held to either of them was in the right.
§2 — A louse on the Sabbath

Of the dissension between them: "Bayt Shammai" forbade killing a louse on the day of the Sabbath, and "Bayt Hillel" permitted it. Those who came later said: we hold the opinion of the school of "Bayt Hillel." They dissented over His saying [Exod 22:4]: "וּמֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם." Some of them said: this refers to the injured party, and so He said "the best of his field" — for he knows that fields and vineyards may contain thorns, brush, much vegetation of trees, reeds, and the like, but also good and precious fruits; so [the owner] is obliged, if he turned his beast loose and it grazed in that good field, to pay for what it grazed and ruined. So His saying "the best" refers to what preceded — the sense being "[the beast] grazed in the best of his field" — and His saying "shall pay" stands by itself. Others said: it refers to the doer [the one who pays].
§3 — The bride-price

Of what is between the people of al-Shām and the people of Iraq of dissension — the people of al-Shām make the bride-price (mohar) for a virgin two hundred zuz, and for a widow one hundred zuz; while the people of Iraq, the bride-price with them is twenty-five zuz. This requires that the marriage of the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, is not a valid marriage — since they do not pay the obligatory bride-price. And if it is a valid marriage, and there is no fixed limit to the bride-price, what is the meaning of "two hundred zuz"? Yet they have said in the "Mishnah" a statement that contradicts the statement of all concerning the bride-price; namely [M. Qiddushin 1:1]: "הָאִישׁ מְקַדֵּשׁ בְּפָרוּטָה אוֹ בִּשְׁוֵה פְּרוּטָה." So if it is permitted for a man to betroth his wife with a single coin (fals), is it not annulled that there is here a limit — neither twenty-five, nor two hundred, neither more nor less?
§4 — A widow and a nursing woman

Of this — that the people of Iraq, if a woman was nursing and her husband died, do not permit her to marry in less than two years; while the people of al-Shām permit her marriage at eighteen months. This requires that the child born to her, with the people of Iraq, is a "child of fornication" (mamzer); for she married upon the forbidden. We have already said before that the people of al-Shām examine by the finger, while with the people of Iraq this is close to lewdness. And of this: that the people of Iraq forbid the one who consummated [marriage] to return to intercourse except after seven days, while the people of al-Shām permit it. If a child came of that intercourse, it is, with the people of Iraq, a "child of fornication." Correspondingly, the people of al-Shām are obliged [to hold] that whoever was made pregnant from the night of consummation — that child must be a "child of fornication"; for consummation, with them, must be only by the finger.
§5 — Cooking on Sabbath eve; the Day of Atonement

Of this: the people of Iraq hold that one may set the pot in the oven before the entry of the Sabbath, so that it cooks on the Sabbath; while the people of al-Shām forbid this. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are Sabbath-profaners without doubt. And of this: the people of Iraq do not wash the hands [after contact with] one who died in their hands, nor [after] contact [with a corpse]; while the people of al-Shām wash the hands of this — even on the Day of Atonement, on which washing is forbidden. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are perpetually impure. One of the elders (shuyūkh) already told me that he saw in the evening people who do not wash the hands [after] contact. I mention this because, if they heard it, they would deny and contradict it — but the truth is sound. And of this: the people of al-Shām purify their hands with water, and the people of Iraq with stones. We have already said that the people of Iraq permit a menstruant to do all the work of the house — cooking, baking, and the rest — while the people of al-Shām forbid this. This is like the foregoing statements.
§6 — The lulav of Booths; circumcision

Of this: the people of Iraq permit, on the day of the Sabbath of the days of the Festival of Booths, [carrying] the myrtle, and forbid the taking of the palm-branch (lulav); while the people of al-Shām hold the contrary. And of this: the people of Iraq permit weighing the meat on the festival-day, while the people of al-Shām forbid putting it on the scales at all, even to guard it from the mouse. So the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, are festival-profaners. And of this: the people of Iraq circumcise with water, the people of al-Shām with earth. So with each group of them, the circumcision of the other group is not a [valid] circumcision.
§7 — Inspecting the lung

Of this: the people of Iraq examine the sheep (the permitted from the forbidden) by inspecting the lung, while the people of al-Shām do so by inspecting the head. An elder of the elders of "al-Raqqa" reported that he had been at the Temple, and that a ewe was inspected by the head and came out forbidden, but inspected by the lung came out permitted; and another ewe was the contrary. So each group of them, with the other group, eats ṭerefah. And of this: the people of Iraq do not hold the slaughter of an animal [valid] until it has been born eight days, while the people of al-Shām slaughter it from its [first] day. So the people of al-Shām, with the people of Iraq, perpetually eat the forbidden. And of this: the people of Iraq do not hold that a woman may be betrothed in the seventh year, while the people of al-Shām hold this. So whoever married in that year, with the people of al-Shām, is not validly married with the people of Iraq, and her children are not legitimate.
§8 — Carrying coins; the festival-day

Of this: the people of Iraq hold that carrying coins is permitted on the Sabbath, while the people of al-Shām forbid even drawing near them. So the people of Iraq, with them, are Sabbath-profaners. And of this: the people of Iraq take the festival for two days, the people of al-Shām for one day. So the people of al-Shām, with the people of Iraq, are festival-profaners, falling under [Deut 13:1]: "וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ"; and the people of Iraq, with the people of al-Shām, take a festival God did not make obligatory, falling under His saying [ibid.]: "לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו."
§9 — Conclusion

All that we have recounted of this — some we took [first-hand], some we learned [by report]. It is found and recorded in their books, and some of them already collected some of it in a separate book, from which we took and learned. So let not [the Rabbanites] busy your hearts with this, nor [should you] turn to it [as a charge against us]; for it is they upon whom the disgrace and the contradiction fell in this — from the very place where they claimed that all that is in their hands is transmitted from prophecy. What is of this kind may admit of no dissension at all; and in the falling of dissension [upon it] is a refutation of the statement of whoever claims this. As for us — we bring forth knowledge by deriving it with our intellects; and what is of this kind, we do not deny that dissension may fall upon it. We shall later recount what the "dissenters" claim in this, by way of reflection, and the answer to all of it.

: The core of Q's argument against the Rabbanites: if their tradition — supposedly solid historiographical truth — was beset by such internal disputes, they cannot claim "the tradition compels [it]." The only truth is that of Karaite "inquiry and reflection." Cf. Astren, History, II.C.

: The rabbinic principle "these and these are the words of the living God" (B. ʿEruvin 13b). Q treats it as a scandal: how can two contradictory statements both be true? Cf. Ben-Shammai, "Scripture and Controversy."
: The dispute over "the best of his field" (Exod 22:4) — whether it refers to the injured party's loss or to the payer; based on M. Bava Qamma 1:1.
: Arabic fals, a copper coin = a perutah.
: Arabic yastanjūn, the cleansing of the hands (istinjāʾ); the Babylonian Rabbanites used stones, the Jerusalemites water.
: Arabic saʿaf al-nakhl, the palm-branch = lulav.
: "al-Raqqa," an old city in northern Syria, a Karaite-Jewish center in this period.
